title: Statistics that want you to panic
intro: The issue's discipline thread: a scary half-year number, an attention-hungry P&L, and two reframes worth keeping.

steps.title: The panic statistic
steps.body:
The Sensex fell **9.7% in H1 2026** — 'the worst first half since 2020, when Covid wiped out 15%.' The piece's point: a statistic like that **has one job — it wants you to panic**: stop the SIP, sell, wait.

> [!warn] Check the construction: 'worst since 2020' *selects* the comparison that maximizes alarm — and the Covid half it cites was followed by one of the strongest recoveries on record. The statistic's own history refutes its advice.

steps.title: The number built for attention
steps.body: Twenty-five years of the same advice: look at your portfolio **less often**. The daily P&L at the top of the screen 'is there to hold your attention rather than inform you' — it measures nothing your plan needs, and it recruits you into reacting.

steps.title: Two reframes
steps.body: Two arguments from the issue's columns that outlast the news cycle they answered:

points.label: Robots & SIPs
points.note: The Musk retort: if machines do the work, wages shrink — OWNING PRODUCTIVE CAPITAL becomes the only claim on what the robots make. A SIP is that claim, bought monthly.

points.label: Recency bias
points.note: The bearish client countering data with other people's gloom — while India adds ~17% of global real GDP growth and sits at ~half China's MSCI EM weight. Mean reversion argues patiently.

steps.title: What discipline actually is
steps.body:
Not stoicism — **structure**: a written allocation, SIPs that continue through scary halves, a rebalance rule that trims doubled winners, and an attention diet that starves the daily number.

The boring machinery does the emotional work so you don't have to.

recap:
**Panic statistics are framings; discipline is structure.**

- 'Worst since X' chooses its window to alarm — its own history usually refutes it.
- The daily P&L is engineered salience; look less often.
- A SIP is a monthly claim on productive capital — more valuable, not less, in an automated future.
- Written rules (allocation, rebalance triggers) beat felt reactions.
